opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the things I find most exciting, because toxicity is really where so many drug programs go to die. You can spend years designing a molecule that binds beautifully to your target, it's potent, it looks great on paper, and then it fails late because it's interacting with something else in the body that you never intended. That's incredibly costly, both in time and money, but more importantly for the patients who are waiting on these medicines.

Historically, the way we've approached toxicity has been quite piecemeal. You'd have specific assays or specific models for particular known liabilities, a handful of off-targets you know to check against, and a lot of it is empirical: you find out when something goes wrong. What changes with general models of molecular interactions is that you're no longer building a narrow predictor for one problem. You have a model that has learned, at a fundamental level, how molecules and proteins come together, how they bind, what the structures look like. Once you have that, toxicity starts to look like the same problem as efficacy, just viewed from the other side. Instead of asking "does my molecule bind the thing I want?", you ask "what else across the proteome might this molecule bind?"

That's a really powerful reframing, because it means you can in principle screen a candidate against a huge number of proteins computationally, early in the design process, before you've ever made the compound. You can start designing for selectivity from day one rather than discovering problems in the clinic. And because these models generalize, you're not limited to the off-targets you already know to worry about; you can surface interactions nobody thought to test.

We're not all the way there yet. Toxicity is also about metabolism, about downstream biology, about things that aren't purely a single binding event. But getting the interaction layer right, in a general way, is the foundation for all of that. And it's the kind of thing that just wasn't possible a few years ago, so being able to work on it now is pretty thrilling.

r001.rationale: The response says toxicity often arises when a drug interacts with something else in the body that it was not intended to bind.

r002.rationale: It proposes using a general interaction model to screen a candidate computationally against a huge number of proteins across the proteome.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that toxicity is where drug discovery actually fails, and it fails late, when it's most expensive. You can have a molecule that binds its target beautifully, and then it goes into animals or into people and it hits something you never thought to look at, a cardiac ion channel, a liver enzyme, some off-target kinase, and years of work and hundreds of millions of dollars are gone. Roughly a third of clinical failures are safety related, and historically our tools for predicting that have been pretty crude: panels of a few dozen known liabilities, some QSAR models that are essentially pattern-matching on chemical substructures, and then a lot of hoping.

What gets me excited about general models of molecular interactions is that they reframe the problem. Instead of asking "does this molecule look like things that were toxic before," you ask "what does this molecule actually do when you drop it into the body." Toxicity isn't a property of a molecule in isolation. It's a property of the molecule interacting with the whole proteome, with everything it might bump into. So if you have a model that has learned, from structure and from binding data, how small molecules and proteins fit together in general, not just for one target you care about, you can in principle screen a candidate against the entire human proteome computationally. You see the off-targets before anyone synthesizes anything.

And the word "general" is doing a lot of work there. The old approach was one model per target, trained on that target's data, which means for the thousands of proteins where you have little or no data you're blind, and those are exactly the surprises that kill programs. A model that has learned the shared physics and chemistry of interaction transfers to those blind spots. That's the thing that wasn't possible even a few years ago.

The other piece is that it changes how you design. Right now toxicity is a filter you apply after the fact. If prediction is good enough and fast enough, it becomes part of the objective. You're optimizing for potency and selectivity and safety simultaneously, in the same loop, rather than discovering the liability at the end. I'd be careful not to oversell it, because we're not there yet, and the biology downstream of binding, metabolism, immune responses, all of that is still hard. But getting the interaction layer right is the foundation, and I think we're genuinely at the point where these models are good enough to start moving the needle.

r001.rationale: The response says a drug can hit unexpected off-target proteins, such as cardiac ion channels, liver enzymes, and kinases, causing toxicity.

r002.rationale: It proposes using a general model of molecule–protein interactions to computationally screen a drug candidate against the entire human proteome.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that toxicity is fundamentally about how a molecule interacts with a biological system, often in ways you didn’t intend. You might design a drug to bind to one particular protein, but it can interact with other proteins as well, and those interactions can lead to side effects.

If you have a general model of molecular interactions, you can start to ask both questions: will this molecule do what we want, and what else might it do? That creates the possibility of identifying problems much earlier and designing molecules with those risks in mind, rather than discovering them late in development.

Of course, predicting an interaction isn’t the same as predicting toxicity in a person. Dose, exposure, metabolism—all of those matter. But a general model could give us a much richer starting point for understanding those effects and deciding which experiments to run.

r001.rationale: The response says a drug can interact with proteins beyond its intended target and that those interactions can cause side effects, connecting unintended interactions to toxicity.

r002.rationale: It proposes using a general interaction model to ask what else a molecule might do, but does not clearly say to predict its interactions with proteins throughout the body.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that toxicity is fundamentally about how a molecule interacts with biology, including all the things you didn’t intend it to interact with. You might design a drug to bind to one particular protein, but that molecule encounters a whole range of other proteins in the body. Some of those interactions could cause problems.

If we can build a general model of molecular interactions, we can start asking those questions much earlier: what else might this molecule bind to, and how could we change it to avoid those interactions while preserving the effect we want? That could help us move beyond discovering a toxicity problem late in development and towards designing better molecules from the outset.

Of course, predicting binding isn’t the same as predicting toxicity. Dose, metabolism, and where the molecule goes in the body all matter. But having a more general understanding of the underlying interactions gives us a powerful foundation to build on.

r001.rationale: The response says toxicity involves unintended interactions with biology and explains that a drug may interact with other proteins, causing problems.

r002.rationale: It proposes using a general model of molecular interactions to predict what else a drug might bind to in the body.
